opus-5.5.text:
I think toy models are indispensable, but you have to be honest about what they're good for and what they aren't.

The reason they're so valuable for degeneracy specifically is that degeneracy is a geometric property of the loss landscape, and in a small enough model you can actually see the geometry. You can write down the set of parameters that achieve minimal loss, understand why it's singular rather than a nice smooth manifold, and compute things like the learning coefficient either exactly or very nearly so. That gives you ground truth. When we develop estimators for quantities from singular learning theory, like the local learning coefficient, the first thing you want to know is whether the estimator recovers the right answer in a case where you already know the answer. Without toy models you're just producing numbers and hoping.

The second thing toy models give you is intuition about mechanism. Take something like the toy models of superposition that Anthropic studied. There you have a clean setting where you can watch the network move between qualitatively different arrangements of features during training, and you can ask whether those transitions line up with changes in the geometry, in the degeneracy of the critical points it's passing near. That turned out to be a really productive way of connecting the abstract theory, phase transitions in the Bayesian posterior, to something concrete you can visualize.

Now, the limitations. The obvious worry is that the kinds of degeneracy you see in a two-layer network with a handful of neurons might not be representative of what's happening in a large transformer. Some degeneracies are generic and come from the architecture itself, symmetries like rescaling between layers or permuting hidden units. Those you'll see everywhere. But the more interesting degeneracy, the kind that reflects what the model has actually learned about the structure of the data, depends heavily on the data distribution, and toy data is by construction impoverished. So there's a real risk of building elaborate intuitions that don't transfer.

My view is that the right way to use them is as calibration rather than as the main event. You use toy models to check that your tools measure what you think they measure, and to generate hypotheses. Then you have to go and test those hypotheses at scale, in real language models, and see whether the story survives. Some of the most encouraging work we've seen is exactly that, where something first understood in a toy setting, like stagewise development showing up in the learning coefficient over training, then also shows up in transformers trained on real data. When that happens, it tells you the toy model was capturing something real rather than being an artifact of its own simplicity.

fable-5.1.text:
Toy models are genuinely useful here, but you have to be honest about what they can and can't tell you, so let me give both sides.

The case for them is that degeneracy is a structural phenomenon, and structure is exactly the thing you can see clearly in a small system. When I say degeneracy, I mean the fact that the map from parameters to the function a network computes is many-to-one in complicated ways. Different parameter settings give you the same or nearly the same behaviour, and the geometry of those sets of equivalent parameters is not simple. They're not just flat valleys. They have singularities, places where the local structure changes character, and that's what singular learning theory is built to describe. In a toy model you can actually write down the loss, compute the real log canonical threshold, and check that the theory is doing what it claims. You can watch a network move from one degenerate region to another during training and verify that the local learning coefficient tracks that. That kind of ground truth is essentially impossible to get in a frontier model, so toy models are where the theory earns its credibility.

The deeper point is that toy models let you separate what is universal from what is incidental. The reason I think degeneracy matters at all is that it's not an artifact of small networks. It comes from the compositional structure of the architecture itself, from the fact that you can permute neurons, rescale between layers, have units that are effectively off, and so on. Those symmetries exist in a two-layer tanh network and they exist in a transformer. So if you understand how degeneracy shapes learning dynamics in the simple case, you have a real hypothesis about the big case, not just an analogy.

Now the cautions. The first is that toy models can mislead you about which degeneracies matter. In a tiny network the dominant singularities often come from things like dead units or exact symmetries that you can enumerate by hand. In a large model trained on real data, the interesting degeneracy is probably mostly about approximate structure, about near-redundancy between many components, and that's much harder to study in a system small enough to fully analyse. There's a risk of building beautiful theory about the wrong singularities.

The second is scale-dependence. Some of the phenomena we care about, like the way a model develops internal structure in stages over training, show up in toy settings, but whether their character is the same at scale is an empirical question. I think the right attitude is to treat toy models as a source of sharp, falsifiable predictions, then go test those with estimators like the local learning coefficient on models that are much too large to analyse directly. If the predictions hold, great. If they break, the toy model has done its job by telling you where your understanding ran out.

So I'd say toy models are indispensable for building the theory and almost useless as the final word. The aim is a ladder, where the toy models give you the concepts and the measurements at scale tell you whether those concepts survive contact with reality. Where I'm optimistic is that so far, the core ideas about degeneracy have survived that climb better than I expected.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very useful, provided you’re clear about what they’re a toy model of. With degeneracy, the basic issue is that different parameter settings can represent the same function, and the geometry around those settings can be much more complicated than a nice, isolated minimum. A toy model lets you examine that geometry in a setting where you can actually calculate something.

For example, you can study a small network where a hidden unit becomes redundant, or where two units effectively do the same thing. Those sound like trivial cases, but they already expose why counting parameters isn’t a satisfactory measure of the complexity of the model. The parameters aren’t all contributing independently to what the network does.

The limitation is that demonstrating a mechanism in a toy model doesn’t tell you how important it is in a large trained network. You need a bridge back to experiments. So I see toy models as a way to develop precise questions and test our mathematical understanding. They’re extremely valuable for that, but they’re the beginning of an explanation, rather than the end.

sol-6.1.text:
I think toy models are extremely useful, provided you’re clear about what they’re supposed to explain. If you want to understand degeneracy, you want examples where you can actually see how different parameter choices represent the same function, and how those redundancies intersect. In a large neural network, that geometry is very difficult to disentangle.

Even a small network can exhibit something quite interesting. Suppose you have two hidden units doing the same thing. You can redistribute their contributions without changing the output. Or a unit’s contribution can vanish, and then some of its parameters cease to matter. Those give you different kinds of degeneracy, and the places where they meet can be particularly important.

The point of the toy model is to make those mechanisms calculable. You can ask what they do to the loss landscape, to the Bayesian posterior, or to the learning dynamics, rather than just saying, ‘Well, there are lots of flat directions.’

But there’s a substantial gap between identifying a mechanism and showing that it explains what happens in a large trained model. So I regard toy models as a way to develop the mathematics and formulate precise hypotheses. Then you have to test whether the structures they isolate are actually the ones that matter at scale.
